sentences.text: The species P. tankei was approximately one-third larger than P. hardiei and possessed a markedly more robust upper arm. The bones of Pasquiaornis resemble those of the mid-sized Baptornis advenus more closely than the large Hesperornis or Parahesperornis.
The discovery of at least three P. hardiei and six P. tankei remains in a limited area suggests either mass mortality events or nearby breeding colonies.
The genus Pasquiaornis contains two species, P. hardiei and P. tankei, which were described in 1997 by Tim Tokaryk, Stephen Cumbaa, and John Storer.

Pasquiaornis appears to be one of the most basal lineages within the Hesperornithes. Pasquiaornis had wings that were poorly adapted for diving compared to other Hesperornithes, and its thickened wing bones were not well suited for flight.
It is unclear but unlikely that Pasquiaornis, or at least P. tankei, was capable of flight.
Pasquiaornis likely fed on fish and marine invertebrates by diving in the Western Interior Seaway.
Later discoveries suggest Pasquiaornis is a basal member of the Hesperornithes, whereas Baptornis represents a more advanced lineage.

Pasquiaornis lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, specifically between 95 and 93 million years ago. The time range for Pasquiaornis is the Cenomanian stage, from 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
